overview:
In Jain philosophy, **greed (lobha)** is one of the central passions (kaṣāyas) that obstructs the soul’s innate purity and contributes to the bondage of karma. It is classified as a major internal enemy because it binds the soul with intense, long‑lasting karmic particles, particularly those associated with delusion (mohanīya karma). Greed manifests as an insatiable desire for possessions, sensory pleasures, status, or control, and is considered more subtle and persistent than anger or pride. Jain thinkers emphasize that greed arises from attachment (rāga) and fuels cycles of accumulation, fear of loss, and unethical behavior.

Across Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrti‑pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—greed is treated as a root cause of suffering because it prevents equanimity (samatā) and non‑possessiveness (aparigraha). The cultivation of aparigraha is not merely a moral ideal but a technical requirement for reducing karmic influx (āsrava) and promoting karmic shedding (nirjarā). Greed is also linked to the lower stages of spiritual development (guṇasthānas), where delusion and attachment dominate. As one progresses, greed becomes increasingly subtle, eventually requiring deep meditative insight to overcome.

Ethically, greed is understood as a driver of violence (hiṃsā), since excessive desire often leads individuals to harm living beings—directly or indirectly—to secure resources or maintain possessions. Jain lay practice therefore includes vows (vratas) and lifestyle disciplines aimed at limiting possessions, consumption, and desires. Modern Jain scholarship also explores greed in the context of consumerism, environmental degradation, and economic inequality, showing how classical teachings remain relevant in contemporary ethical debates.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.3 lists greed as one of the four primary passions (anger, pride, deceit, greed) that bind destructive karma. Commentaries across traditions agree that greed is the most persistent and subtle of the four.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to early Śvetāmbara canonical compilers
primary_sources.translation: Greed is the cause of suffering.
primary_sources.notes: This passage appears in teachings on renunciation and the dangers of attachment. The text emphasizes that greed leads to restlessness, fear, and moral downfall.

primary_sources.title: Daśavaikālika Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.translation: The vow of non‑possessiveness is for the cessation of greed.
primary_sources.notes: This passage links ethical vows directly to the reduction of greed. It is frequently cited in lay practice guides.

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama (Digambara)
primary_sources.author: Puṣpadanta and Bhūtabali
primary_sources.translation: Karmic bondage arises from attachment and similar passions.
primary_sources.notes: Although not naming greed explicitly in this line, Digambara commentaries clarify that lobha is a primary form of rāga contributing to karmic bondage.

misconceptions.myth: Greed only refers to material possessions.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts define greed broadly as any excessive desire—including for praise, influence, sensory pleasure, or even spiritual attainments. It is an inner passion, not merely a financial attitude.

misconceptions.myth: Greed can be eliminated simply by giving away possessions.
misconceptions.reality: Jain philosophy emphasizes that greed is a mental state. Reducing possessions helps, but true elimination requires inner transformation through meditation, vows, and cultivation of equanimity.

misconceptions.myth: Greed is less harmful than anger or pride.
misconceptions.reality: Many Jain commentaries describe greed as the most persistent and subtle passion, capable of binding karma for long durations because it often operates quietly and continuously.
